processing: One 2014 newspaper article, itself drawing on an online encyclopedia, gives the only method found: fresh leaf is boiled or steamed soft, rubbed on a bamboo mat, packed hard into a large bamboo tube and drained upside down. After two days the tube is sealed with ash mud for two to three months, until the leaf yellows. The leaf is then dried, jarred and steeped in sesame oil.
appearance_dry: Pickled teas of this kind are not dry at all: expect moist, dark olive leaf.
appearance_liquor: Usually eaten rather than brewed, so there is no characteristic liquor; a brew from similar sour teas is yellow to amber.
appearance_wet: Moist, soft, dark olive leaves, as is typical of pickled teas.
taste_profile: No tasting record specific to this tea exists. Pickled teas of the region are generally sour and savoury, with a bitter edge.

brewing.notes: Mostly a food, so brewing is the exception. In this region, pickled tea is usually dressed like a salad; a hot infusion is only an approximation.

vintage_note: It is a home or village food, not a retail tea sold by vintage. Nothing is documented about seasons or ageing for this particular tea, and with other pickled teas freshness and clean fermentation matter more than a year on the label.
description:
Jingpo pickled tea is a tea food of the Jingpo people of Dehong, in western Yunnan. Very little has been written about it, and the one account found is a newspaper piece of modest authority.

In that account, softened fresh leaf is packed into a bamboo tube, sealed for two to three months until it yellows, then dried and kept in sesame oil.

It is eaten more than drunk, either straight as a dish or stir-fried with garlic and other seasonings. Teas of this family are generally sour with bitterness behind, though no tasting record exists for this one.

De'ang sour tea from the same prefecture is a separate tea with a similar bamboo-tube fermentation. If you meet Jingpo tea in Dehong, ask how it was made and how long it was sealed, and do not assume a jar labelled pickled tea elsewhere is the same thing.
history: Little is documented. No dated account or named maker is on record for Jingpo pickled tea, and it should not be confused with De'ang sour tea, whose making is listed as intangible heritage.
